Conceive
kun-SEEV
v.
Latin concipere: con- (together) + capere (to take)—to take together, to take in. The same verb covers the womb that takes in seed and the heart that takes in a purpose, which is exactly the double use Scripture makes of it.

Biblical Definition

Scripture uses conceive of the womb and of the heart, and treats the two as one kind of act. In the womb: a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel (Isa 7:14), fulfilled in Gabriel's word to Mary, thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son (Luke 1:31). Conception in the Bible is never a merely biological event; it is the point at which God's purpose takes hold in a body. Sarah conceives by promise, Hannah by answered prayer, Elisabeth in old age, Mary by the Holy Ghost. In the heart the same verb runs its darker course: when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death (Jas 1:15). Job says of the wicked, they conceive mischief, and bring forth vanity (Job 15:35). Sin has a gestation. It is conceived in secret, carried, and delivered, and James traces the whole pregnancy so that a man will recognize the early stage rather than only the birth. David confesses conception itself as the point where his sinfulness begins: in sin did my mother conceive me (Ps 51:5). So the word ties together the doctrine of the image, the doctrine of original sin, and the incarnation itself—each turning on what is taken in and what is brought forth.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines CONCEIVE as to receive into the womb and become pregnant; and figuratively, to form in the mind, to imagine, devise, or purpose.

expand to see more

CONCEIVE, v.t. — To receive into the womb and breed; to begin the formation of the embryo. She shall conceive and bear a son.

CONCEIVE, v.t. — To form in the mind; to imagine; to devise; to purpose. Hence, to conceive mischief is to devise evil in the heart before it is done.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 7:14 — "Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel."

Luke 1:31 — "And, behold, thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son, and shalt call his name JESUS."

James 1:15 — "Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death."

Job 15:35 — "They conceive mischief, and bring forth vanity, and their belly prepareth deceit."

Modern Corruption

Conception has been reduced to a medical event with no moral or covenantal weight, while the heart-sense has been abandoned entirely—leaving no vocabulary for the truth that sin, like a child, is conceived long before it is delivered.

expand to see more

Modern speech keeps conceive almost exclusively as a clinical term: a procedure succeeded, a cycle worked, a pregnancy was achieved. What drops out is that Scripture treats conception as the moment a person begins and a purpose of God takes hold in a body. Once conception is only biology, the question of what is conceived becomes a matter of preference and timing, and the language required to say otherwise has already been surrendered.

The heart-sense is nearly extinct, and its loss costs the church real ground in the fight against sin. James is precise: lust conceives, carries, and delivers. A man who only recognizes sin at the delivery—the act, the scandal, the fallout—is fighting far too late. The older usage let a man say plainly that he had conceived a bitterness, an adultery, a revenge, weeks before anything was done, and repent at that stage. Recovering the word recovers the early warning.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew harah, to conceive or be with child, used of wombs and of wicked schemes alike; Greek syllambanō, to take together, to conceive.

expand to see more

Hebrew harah (H2029) — to conceive, become pregnant; also used of conceiving mischief or trouble in the heart (Gen 4:1; Ps 7:14; Isa 7:14; 59:4).

Greek syllambanō (G4815) — to take together, seize; hence to conceive in the womb (Luke 1:24, 31, 36) and, in James, of lust conceiving (Jas 1:15).

Greek gennao (G1080) — to beget or bring forth, the delivery that follows conception (Matt 1:20; Jas 1:15 context).

Usage

"A virgin shall conceive—the incarnation itself hangs on this verb."

"James 1:15 gives sin a full pregnancy: conceived by lust, carried, delivered as death."

"Job's wicked conceive mischief—the heart is a womb, and it is never idle."
